title: Billy Evans Slams Amanda Seyfried, Nathan Fielder: “It’s My Life and I Love It” – THR Exclusive
body:
In a candid, first‑ever print interview about the upcoming docuseries *You Can See Everything*, Billy Evans—who has been identified publicly as the longtime partner of former Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes—bristled at recent portrayals that paint him as a manipulative opportunist. Speaking to a leading entertainment outlet, Evans pushed back against actress Amanda Seyfried’s comments, which he says were part of a broader effort to “tear us apart,” and he used the moment to reiterate his devotion to his own life and to the narrative he believes the series will finally set straight.

Evans, a former tech‑industry consultant turned private investor, has largely stayed out of the spotlight since Holmes’ 2022 conviction. When *You Can See Everything*—co‑created by comedian‑producer Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim—announced that it would feature unprecedented access to Evans and Holmes, speculation ran rampant about whether the series would serve as a redemption arc or a fresh exposé. Evans now claims the project is precisely the latter: a chance to “reset the public’s perception” of Holmes, who he describes as “a brilliant, misunderstood entrepreneur who was unfairly vilified.” He insists that the documentary will reveal “the human side of a story that has been reduced to headlines and memes.”

The tension between Evans and Seyfried stems from the actress’s recent interview in which she, playing a fictionalized version of a journalist in the series, suggested that Evans had been “instrumental in keeping Holmes isolated” and that his influence was “toxic.” Seyfried, who also serves as an executive producer on the series, said her comments were meant to “highlight the complexities of power dynamics in high‑profile relationships.” Evans, however, interpreted the remarks as a direct attack. “It feels like a coordinated attempt to rewrite history and paint us as villains,” he said, adding that he and Holmes have “weathered far worse than media speculation.”

Industry insiders note that the clash is emblematic of a larger debate over documentary ethics. Fielder, known for his satirical approach on *Nathan for You*, has promised a “hybrid” format that blends investigative journalism with staged reenactments. Critics worry this could blur the line between fact and fiction, especially when subjects like Evans are both participants and subjects. “When a filmmaker is also a producer, there’s an inherent conflict of interest,” said media analyst Priya Desai. “The audience must remain vigilant about whose narrative is being amplified.”

Beyond the personal drama, Evans disclosed a surprising detail about the series’ most talked‑about moment: a nude scene involving Holmes. According to Evans, the scene was not intended to be titillating but rather to symbolize vulnerability and the stripping away of the mythos that has surrounded Holmes for years. “It’s about confronting the raw truth of who she is, beyond the courtroom and the headlines,” he explained. He also emphasized that the decision was made collaboratively, with Holmes herself approving the artistic direction.

While the interview did not reveal a release date, Evans hinted that the series could debut as early as next spring on a major streaming platform. He expressed optimism that the final product will “challenge the audience to rethink what they think they know” and perhaps spark a broader conversation about the treatment of women in tech, the media’s role in shaping public opinion, and the ethics of documentary storytelling.

As the buzz around *You Can See Everything* builds, the clash between Evans and Seyfried may prove to be a microcosm of the larger cultural reckoning the series hopes to ignite. Whether the documentary succeeds in reshaping Holmes’ legacy—or simply adds another layer to an already complex saga—remains to be seen. What is clear, however, is that Evans is determined to steer the narrative, and his forthcoming appearance on screen could mark a pivotal moment in the ongoing debate over truth, power, and redemption in the age of streaming.
